u7-l01.title: The attraction
u7-l01.summary: Drawing a piece to the square you want

u7-l01-s01.text: White has two rooks on the e-file. With Rxf8+ they sacrifice the one on e8: the king captures it because it has no other way out, and ends up on f8. Then the other rook gives mate on e8, protected by the knight. That's an attraction: a sacrifice, almost always with check, that pulls the king or another piece to a square where it takes the blow.

u7-l01-s02.text: The attraction also sets up other tactics. Here the white queen captures the black queen on h8 with check. The king recaptures and lands on h8, right where the knight checks it and attacks the rook on e7 at the same time. You traded queen for queen, but you win a rook.

u7-l01-s03.prompt: What is the sacrifice Rxf8+ for?
options: To pull the king to f8, where it gets mated
To win a rook for nothing
To trade the rooks and simplify
u7-l01-s03.explanation: The rook is given up to force the king to capture: on f8 it has no free squares and the other rook gives mate.
feedback: The king captures it, so you don't win the rook: you win the mate.
Nothing gets simplified: the sacrifice forces a sequence that ends in mate.

u7-l01-s04.prompt: If you play Rxf8+, the king has to capture. Tap the square where it will end up.
u7-l01-s04.hint: It's the square of the rook you sacrifice.

u7-l01-s05.prompt: Sacrifice the bishop with check to pull the king over and win the bishop on c8.
u7-l01-s05.hint: The bishop steps aside with check, the king captures and the rook on c1 ends up attacking c8.
u7-l01-s05.success: Correct. Bxe8+ pulls the king to e8. With the bishop off the c-file, the rook wins the bishop on c8 with check.

u7-l01-s06.prompt: Sacrifice a rook with check to pull the king over and give mate in two.
u7-l01-s06.hint: Look at the first rank: one rook is given up so the king captures and the other gives mate.
u7-l01-s06.success: Correct. Rxe1+ forces the king to capture and Rd1# is mate.

u7-l02-s01.text: The black queen defends both the knight on d5 and the bishop on e7: it has two jobs. If you capture the knight, the queen recaptures and leaves the bishop undefended. That wins you a piece. That's an overload: an enemy piece with more work than it can handle.

u7-l02-s02.text: The black rook on f8 defends the rook on e8 and the pawn on f7. With Bxf7+ you give check. If the rook on f8 captures the bishop, it no longer protects the rook on e8 and Qxe8+ wins it.

u7-l02-s03.prompt: The black queen defends two pieces that can fall. Tap those two pieces.
u7-l02-s03.hint: One is on the queen's file and the other on its diagonal.

u7-l02-s04.prompt: Why is it a good idea to capture the knight on d5?
options: Because if the queen recaptures, it leaves the bishop on e7 undefended
Because the knight on d5 is worth more than my knight
Because it opens the d-file for my rook
u7-l02-s04.explanation: The black queen defends both pieces: by recapturing on d5 it abandons the bishop on e7.
feedback: Both knights are worth the same: what matters is what the recapture leaves undefended.
Opening the file isn't the point: what counts is that the queen can't defend both pieces.

u7-l02-s05.prompt: Look for the capture that forces an enemy piece to recapture and leaves another one undefended.
u7-l02-s05.hint: Look for an enemy piece that defends two things at once: capture one and win the other.
u7-l02-s05.success: Correct. Rxe1 forces the defending piece to recapture, and you win the other one.

u7-l03-s01.text: The black queen captured on d4. If you recapture right away with Qxd4, the knight on c6 recaptures and you've only traded queens. First you play Bxc6+: you give check and capture the knight. If Black answers with bxc6, you capture the queen with Qxd4 and there is no knight left to recapture. That's an in-between move: a check or a threat you make before the obvious recapture.

u7-l03-s02.text: The same with Black: the white queen captured on d5. Recapturing right away with Qxd5 allows Nxd5. First, Bxc3+ gives check and removes the knight that protected d5. After bxc3 you can capture the queen.

u7-l03-s03.prompt: Black captured on d4 with the queen. What should you do first?
options: Recapture right away with the queen
Give check with the bishop, capturing the knight on c6
Retreat the queen to a safe square
u7-l03-s03.explanation: With the check you force your opponent to answer and you remove the knight that protected d4. Then you recapture the queen without losing anything.
feedback: If you recapture right away, the knight on c6 recaptures the queen: you'll only have traded queens.
Retreating loses the chance to win the black queen.

u7-l03-s04.prompt: Before recapturing, see who protects the black queen on d4. Tap that piece.
u7-l03-s04.hint: It's a knight that defends it from a nearby square.

u7-l03-s05.prompt: Before recapturing, look for a capture with check.
u7-l03-s05.hint: One of your pieces can capture with check and remove the defender before you take the queen.
u7-l03-s05.success: Correct. Nxf6+ is the in-between move: it is played before recapturing.

u7-l03-s06.hint: Give a check your opponent has to answer before you recapture your piece.
u7-l03-s06.success: Correct. Rxd1+ is the in-between move: it is played before recapturing.

u7-l04.title: The interference
u7-l04.summary: Cutting the defense in the middle

u7-l04-s01.text: The white queen on d1 protects the rook on h1 along the first rank. With Qg2+ the king is forced to go to e1, and it ends up right between the two pieces: it cuts the defense. Then Qxh1+ wins the rook. That's an interference: something gets in between a piece and the piece that protects it.

u7-l04-s02.text: Black has a rook on h8 that the queen on d8 protects along the 8th rank. With Qg7+ the king is forced to go to e8: it steps in between the queen and the rook and separates them. After Qxh8+ Black loses the rook.

u7-l04-s03.prompt: The white queen on d1 protects the rook on h1 along the first rank. What happens if the white king stands on e1?
options: The rook is left unprotected
The rook is better protected
Nothing changes
u7-l04-s03.explanation: The king on e1 blocks the rank: the queen no longer sees the rook and it can be captured for free.
feedback: The king doesn't protect the rook from e1: it gets in the way and cuts the queen's line.
A lot changes: the king blocks the line between the two pieces.

u7-l04-s04.prompt: After Qg2+ the white king has to go to e1. Tap the two white pieces its interference separates.
u7-l04-s04.hint: They are the two pieces on the first rank that protected each other.

u7-l04-s05.prompt: Give a check that forces the king to step between two pieces that protect each other.
u7-l04-s05.hint: Look at the first rank: two rooks protect each other. A queen check can send the king into the middle.
u7-l04-s05.success: Correct. Qd2+ forces the king to cut off its own defense.

u7-l04-s06.hint: Look at the 8th rank: one piece protects another from a distance. A check can send the king into the middle.
u7-l04-s06.success: Correct. Qg7+ forces the king to cut off its own defense.

u7-l05.title: One-piece mates
u7-l05.summary: One piece delivers the final blow

u7-l05-s01.text: The black king has no free squares: its own pawns on f7, g7 and h7 close off the second rank. The rook captures on e8 and gives mate on the back rank. It's the back-rank mate, and a single piece delivers it.

u7-l05-s02.text: The white king is boxed in by its own rook on g1 and the pawns on g2 and h2. The knight gives check from f2 and the king has nowhere to go and can't capture it. It's the smothered mate: only the knight jumps over the other pieces.

u7-l05-s03.prompt: What would have prevented the back-rank mate?
options: A gap for the king, by moving a pawn such as h7 or g7
Trade the queens
Move the rook from a8
u7-l05-s03.explanation: A gap on the second rank gives the king an escape square. A pawn moved in time prevents the mate.
feedback: With the queens traded, the king still has no free squares.
The rook on a8 can't help: the mate comes along the e-file.

u7-l05-s04.prompt: The white king can't move. Tap the three white pieces that block its way.
u7-l05-s04.hint: They're right next to the king: a rook and two pawns.

u7-l05-s05.prompt: Give mate with a single piece: the king is boxed in by its own pieces.
u7-l05-s05.hint: Look for the piece that can give check without the king capturing it or escaping.
u7-l05-s05.success: Correct. Nf7# is mate: the king has no free squares.

u7-l06-s01.text: The queen alone couldn't give this mate: the king would capture it. But the bishop on c4 protects g8 along the same diagonal. When one piece attacks and another supports it on the same line, they form a battery: the king can't capture the queen and has no free squares.

u7-l06-s02.text: This is the Arabian mate: the rook gives check from h7 and the knight on f6 protects it and also covers g8. The king can't capture the rook or escape.

u7-l06-s03.prompt: Which piece stops the black king from capturing the queen on g8?
options: The white bishop on c4
The white king on a2
The white pawn on b2
u7-l06-s03.explanation: The bishop protects g8 along the diagonal: if the king captures the queen, it ends up in check.
feedback: The white king is too far away to protect g8.
The pawn on b2 has nothing to do with g8.

u7-l06-s04.hint: One is a rook and the other a knight.

u7-l06-s05.hint: One piece gives check and the other covers the king's escape squares.
u7-l06-s05.success: Correct. Bxa3# is mate thanks to the other piece, which covers the escape squares.

u7-l06-s06.prompt: Give mate with two pieces working together.
u7-l06-s06.hint: One piece gives check and the other supports it so the king can't capture it.
u7-l06-s06.success: Correct. Qh7# is mate: the other piece supports the queen.

u6-l03-s01.text: Remember the values: a rook is worth 5, and a bishop or knight 3. Trading a rook for a bishop or knight is called “losing the exchange.” Sometimes it pays to do it on purpose: that's an exchange sacrifice.

u6-l03-s02.prompt: If you trade your rook for a knight, about how many points of material do you give up?
u6-l03-s02.explanation: A rook is worth 5 and a knight 3: you give up about 2 points. That's why the sacrifice has to give you something in return.
feedback: Rook 5 minus knight 3 is 2 points, not 1.
Rook 5 minus knight 3 is 2 points, not 3.

u6-l03-s03.text: There are three typical reasons to give up the exchange: to create a passed pawn nobody can stop, to break open the enemy king's defense, or to remove a piece that defends something important. Here, the knight on d6 is the only thing stopping your pawn on c6.

u6-l03-s04.prompt: White to move. Give up the exchange so your pawn can promote.
u6-l03-s04.success: Well solved: this position comes from a real game.
u6-l03-s04.hint: The knight on d6 stops your c-pawn. What happens if you remove it, even if it costs you the rook?

u6-l03-s05.prompt: White to move. Once again: the exchange for an unstoppable pawn.
u6-l03-s05.success: Well solved: this position comes from a real game.
u6-l03-s05.hint: Which black piece stops your b-pawn? Remove it with the rook.

u6-l03-s06.text: The second reason: exposing the king. If your rook captures a piece that protects the enemy king, your other pieces can come in and attack it.

u6-l03-s07.prompt: White to move. Give up the exchange to attack the king.
u6-l03-s07.success: Well solved: this position comes from a real game.
u6-l03-s07.hint: The bishop on g7 protects the black king. Capture it with the rook, then come in with the queen.

u6-l03-s08.prompt: White to move. Remove the defender: the exchange in return for winning more material.
u6-l03-s08.success: Well solved: this position comes from a real game.
u6-l03-s08.hint: The knight on f6 defends the rook on d5. If the knight disappears, the rook is left undefended.

u6-l03-s09.text: To sum up: the exchange is worth about 2 points, but a pawn that promotes, an attack on the king or winning another piece are worth more. Before giving it up, calculate what you get in return.

u7-l07.title: Sacrificing to open up the king
u7-l07.summary: Giving up material to get at the king

u7-l07-s01.text: The pawns on h6 and g7 protect the king. With Rxh6+ you give up the rook: the g7 pawn has to capture, the king is left exposed and the queen gives mate on h6. You're not giving material away: you calculate all the way to the mate before you sacrifice.

u7-l07-s02.text: Here the sacrifice is on g6. With Rxg6+ the rook is offered. If the f7 pawn captures, the king loses its protection and the queen gives mate on g6.

u7-l07-s03.prompt: What does the sacrifice Rxh6+ achieve?
options: It removes a pawn that protected the king and lets the queen in
It wins material right away
It trades the rooks
u7-l07-s03.explanation: The rook is given up to break the king's pawn shield. If the pawn captures, the queen gives mate.
feedback: The sacrifice doesn't win material: you lose a rook in exchange for the mate.
There is no rook trade: your opponent can't recapture with a rook.

u7-l07-s05.success: Correct. Qxh6+ opens the way to the king and the mate comes on the next move.

u7-l08.title: Calculating: mate in two and in three
u7-l08.summary: Look at the checks and follow the sequence

u7-l08-s01.text: To find a mate in two, start with the checks. Here there is only one, Rh8+, and it leaves the black king a single escape: e7. After that, Re8 is mate, with the bishop on c6 protecting the rook.

u7-l08-s02.text: In a mate in three, each check leaves your opponent very few replies, and those are the ones you have to calculate. Here Qd8+ leaves only two replies: interpose the bishop on e8 or the rook on f8. With the bishop, Qxe8+ forces the rook to interpose and Qxf8 is mate.

u7-l08-s03.prompt: After Qd8+, how many legal replies does Black have?
u7-l08-s03.explanation: Only two: interpose the bishop on e8 or the rook on f8. With so few replies you can calculate the whole mate.
feedback: Count again: the king can't move, so the only options are to interpose or capture.
